lessons.title: Collectivisation and the War on the Kulaks

before.content_html:
In 1928 Stalin abandoned the NEP. The Five Year Plans needed grain to feed the cities and to export for foreign currency, and the peasants were not delivering enough. Stalin’s solution was to take farming out of peasant hands altogether. The result, between 1929 and 1933, was the most violent transformation of rural Europe in modern history: an estimated five to seven million dead, a famine that ravaged Ukraine and Kazakhstan, and the destruction of an entire way of life.

The ‘Great Turn’ of 1928

By 1927 a ‘grain procurement crisis’ meant the state was buying about 25 per cent less grain than the year before. Bukharin argued for higher prices and continued NEP. Stalin instead drove a hard line: peasants were hoarding grain, and the Five Year Plans could not wait. The Great Turn of 1928 ended the NEP and committed the state to forced industrialisation paid for by squeezing the countryside.

How Collectivisation Worked

Collectivisation meant peasants surrendered their land, livestock and tools to a collective. Two structures dominated:

  • The kolkhoz: a notionally cooperative collective farm. Peasants worked the land together; the state took a fixed quota first, then peasants were paid in kind from what remained. They kept tiny private plots.
  • The sovkhoz: a state farm where peasants were paid wages like factory workers; less common but more directly state-run.

Tractors, ploughs and other machinery were concentrated in Machine Tractor Stations (MTS), which hired equipment to the kolkhozes for a fee paid in grain. Each MTS had a political department that watched the surrounding farms. The state could reach into rural Russia in a way the Tsars never had.

Key Fact

Collectivisation merged peasant farms into kolkhozes (cooperative collectives) and sovkhozes (state farms). Machine Tractor Stations supplied equipment and political surveillance, giving the state direct control of grain extraction.

Dekulakisation

In December 1929 Stalin called for ‘the liquidation of the kulaks as a class’. The kulak label, which had once meant a richer peasant employing labour, was now applied to almost anyone resisting collectivisation. A peasant with one extra cow, two horses, or a metal roof could be denounced. Roughly a fifth of dekulakised families were executed or sent to forced-labour colonies; another two thirds were deported to Siberia, the Urals or Kazakhstan. Over five million people were affected.

The label was politically constructed. Local activists faced quotas: each district had to find its kulaks. As one historian put it, the dekulakisation campaign was less a war on rich peasants than a quota-driven assault on the most successful tenth of the village.

Peasants resisted in ways open to the powerless. Many slaughtered their livestock rather than hand it over: between 1929 and 1933, USSR cattle stocks fell from about 70 million head to 38 million, sheep and goats from 147 million to 50 million, horses from 33 million to 16 million. Peasants buried grain, broke tools, or fled to the cities. Stalin briefly retreated in March 1930 with his article ‘Dizzy with Success’, blaming over-zealous local officials for ‘excesses’ — but the policy resumed within months.

The Famine of 1932-1933

By 1932 sown area had collapsed and grain output was below 1928 levels — yet state procurement quotas were raised, partly to fund industrial imports. The collision produced famine. The hardest-hit areas were Ukraine, the North Caucasus and Kazakhstan. In Ukraine, where the famine is now called the Holodomor (‘death by hunger’), about four million people died. In Kazakhstan, around 1.5 million Kazakhs — nearly a quarter of the population — died as nomadic herding was destroyed and forced settlement disrupted the seasonal grazing on which Kazakh life depended.

Soviet authorities denied the famine externally and prevented peasants from leaving the affected regions through internal passport controls (introduced December 1932). The Soviet press carried no reports; foreign journalists in Moscow who tried to investigate, such as the Welshman Gareth Jones, were dismissed and discredited by colleagues. Survivors described eating bark, weeds, leather and, in extreme cases, human corpses. Whether Stalin deliberately engineered the Ukrainian famine to crush Ukrainian national identity, or whether it was a product of brutal policy without specific genocidal intent, remains debated. Many historians, the Ukrainian state and several governments now classify the Holodomor as genocide; Russian and some Western historians question the deliberate-targeting argument while accepting Stalin’s responsibility for mass death.

In political terms, yes — the state could now extract grain at will, fund industrial imports, and control the countryside. By 1936, around 90 per cent of peasants worked on collective farms. In agricultural terms, no — Soviet grain output did not regain 1928 levels for decades. Livestock numbers took even longer to recover. Examiner reports flag students who write ‘collectivisation succeeded’ without distinguishing between political control (the regime won) and productivity (the regime lost).

Key Fact

The 1932-33 famine killed roughly four million Ukrainians (the Holodomor) and around 1.5 million Kazakhs. Causes included raised grain quotas, peasant resistance through livestock slaughter, and internal passports introduced in December 1932 that prevented escape from famine zones.
before.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports repeatedly flag the ‘all kulaks were rich’ misconception — demonstrate you know the label was applied loosely. For 8-mark Explain Effects on collectivisation, build the chain end-of-NEP → quotas → resistance → livestock slaughter → famine → political control rather than listing changes. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, contrast totalitarian readings (Stalin engineered the famine) with revisionist accounts (chaotic policy with disastrous results) — and reach a substantiated judgement.

lessons.title: The Five Year Plans and Soviet Society

before.content_html:
In ten years, the Soviet Union became the world’s third-largest industrial economy. Cities, dams, blast furnaces and metro lines were built almost from scratch. The cost was paid in long shifts, accidents, gulag labour and the rationing of food during the 1932-33 famine. To answer ‘were the Five Year Plans a success?’ in the exam, you have to weigh the headline tonnage gains against the quality, the people and the price.

Aims of the Five Year Plans

Stalin set out three core aims for industrialisation. First, build heavy industry — coal, iron, steel, oil — the foundation of any modern economy. Second, achieve autarky: the USSR must produce inside its own borders everything it might need. Third, prepare for war. Stalin told a 1931 audience: ‘We are fifty or a hundred years behind the advanced countries. We must close this gap in ten years. Either we do it, or they crush us.’

First Five Year Plan, 1928-1932

The First Five Year Plan prioritised coal, steel, oil and electricity. Targets were unrealistic; results in heavy industry were nevertheless dramatic. Coal output rose from 35 to 64 million tonnes, steel from 4 to 6 million tonnes, electricity nearly tripled. Consumer goods barely registered. Showcase projects launched in this period include Magnitogorsk — a giant steel city built in the Urals from 1929, designed by American engineers, peopled in part by deported peasants — and the Dnieper Dam, opened in 1932 as Europe’s largest hydroelectric station.

Second Five Year Plan, 1933-1937

The Second Plan continued heavy industry but added transport (the Moscow Metro opened in 1935) and consumer goods. Mining and engineering grew rapidly. Steel hit roughly 18 million tonnes by 1937. Showcase achievements: the White Sea Canal, dug almost entirely by gulag prisoners with around 25,000 deaths during construction, and the Moscow Metro, with stations made deliberately monumental as a public showcase of socialism.

Third Five Year Plan, 1938-1941

The Third Plan turned to armaments and was interrupted by Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. Tank, aircraft and weapons production became a priority — a shift that paid off when the German invasion came. By 1940, military spending had risen to almost a third of state expenditure.

Key Fact

Each Plan had a showcase project. First Plan: Magnitogorsk and the Dnieper Dam. Second Plan: the White Sea Canal (gulag-built) and the Moscow Metro. Third Plan: tank and aircraft production for the coming war.

Workers’ Lives

Soviet workers paid for the Plans in long hours, brutal discipline and frequent accidents. Lateness of more than 20 minutes became a criminal offence in 1940. Internal passports from December 1932 controlled urban residence; collective farmers could not leave the kolkhoz without permission. Wages were tied to output through piece-rates. Crash construction meant accidents were endemic and quality was poor — whole factories were built on bog, while others produced steel that rusted within months.

Yet propaganda celebrated the worker as the hero of socialism. In August 1935, the miner Alexei Stakhanov reportedly cut 102 tonnes of coal in a single shift — fourteen times the norm. The figure was real but engineered: he had teams clearing the coal away. The myth that grew around him — the Stakhanovite movement — pressured workers to exceed norms, with rewards (housing, holidays, bonuses) for top performers and risks for those who fell behind.

The Plans drew women into industry on a scale unseen elsewhere. Female factory employment rose from about 3 million in 1928 to 13 million by 1940; women became a majority of the medical profession. State nurseries, free education and literacy programmes lifted women’s status in real ways. The 1936 Constitution proclaimed equality. Yet women still did the cooking, queuing and childcare on top of their factory shift — the ‘double burden’. Family law tightened in 1936: abortion was banned and divorce made harder, partly to drive up the birth rate after the famine.

City Dwellers and Professionals

The 1920s urban culture of free speech and open debate was crushed. New apartment blocks went up, but the housing shortage meant most workers lived in barracks or shared single rooms in ‘communal’ flats. Professionals — engineers, doctors, planners — were given privileges (better housing, dachas, food access) but were also targeted in ‘wrecking’ trials when projects went wrong, including the Shakhty trial of 1928 that scapegoated mining engineers for the failures of the First Plan.

Were the Plans a Success?

Examiner reports flag this as the recurring weak point in answers. The honest answer is: depends on the metric.

In headline tonnage, yes. By 1940 the USSR was a major industrial power, the world’s third-largest after the US and Germany. The Plans gave the country the steel and weapons that survived Barbarossa. Against the metric of preparing for war — Stalin’s explicit aim — they worked. But quality was often poor: tractors broke; steel cracked; new plants ran far below capacity. Quotas were sometimes met by including gulag output and falsifying figures. Consumer goods (clothes, shoes, kitchenware) remained scarce throughout the 1930s. The Plans were a triumph of headline numbers and a failure of living standards. Top-band 12-mark answers reach a substantiated overall judgement that names which metric they are weighing — not just ‘successful in some ways and not in others’.

Key Fact

By 1940, Soviet industrial output had roughly tripled and the USSR was the world’s third-largest economy. But headline tonnage gains hid quality failures, gulag labour disguised in totals, and consumer poverty. The Plans succeeded against Stalin’s war-preparation aim and failed against worker living standards.
before.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark Period Essays on whether the Plans succeeded, examiner reports praise students who name the metric they are weighing — tonnage, war preparation, living standards, quality — rather than concluding ‘successful in some ways and not others’. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, totalitarian readings (Stalin personally drove the modernisation) clash with revisionist accounts that stress workers, foreign engineers and forced labourers. Always cite a specific tonnage, project name (Magnitogorsk, Dnieper Dam, White Sea Canal) or year — precision earns marks.

lessons.title: Terror, Purges and the Cult of Stalin

before.content_html:
Between 1936 and 1938 Stalin systematically destroyed his own party, his army officer corps, and millions of ordinary citizens. The peak years of the Great Terror — sometimes called the ‘Yezhovshchina’ — saw roughly 750,000 people shot and over a million sent to forced-labour camps. Why this happened, and how much was Stalin’s personal will, is one of the most contested questions in Soviet history.

The Trigger: the Murder of Kirov

On 1 December 1934, Sergei Kirov, the popular Leningrad party chief, was shot dead at the Smolny Institute by a young dissident, Leonid Nikolaev. Stalin used the murder as proof that hidden enemies were active inside the party. The same day, a decree authorised summary trials and execution of suspected terrorists. Whether Stalin himself ordered the killing remains debated — the totalitarian school argues yes, revisionists say a deranged loner is sufficient. Either way, Kirov’s death triggered the wave of arrests that culminated in the Great Terror.

The Show Trials of the Old Bolsheviks, 1936-1938

Between August 1936 and March 1938, three great Moscow show trials destroyed the surviving leadership of the October Revolution.

  • August 1936 — the ‘Trial of the Sixteen’: Zinoviev, Kamenev and 14 others confessed to plotting with Trotsky to murder Stalin and Kirov. All were shot.
  • January 1937 — the ‘Trial of the Seventeen’: Karl Radek and Yuri Pyatakov among them. Most shot.
  • March 1938 — the ‘Trial of the Twenty-One’: Bukharin, the leading Bolshevik intellectual and former defender of the NEP, confessed and was executed. So was Yagoda, the former NKVD chief.

Confessions were extracted by sleep deprivation, threats to families and prolonged interrogation. The trials were a public theatre: foreign journalists were allowed in to watch defendants admit to fantastic crimes. Western observers split — some accepted the confessions, others (including the philosopher John Dewey’s commission) denounced them as fabrications. Modern historians treat the confessions as forced.

Key Fact

Three Moscow show trials destroyed the Old Bolshevik leadership: the Trial of the Sixteen (Aug 1936, Zinoviev and Kamenev shot), the Trial of the Seventeen (Jan 1937), and the Trial of the Twenty-One (Mar 1938, Bukharin shot). Confessions were extracted by torture and threats to families.

Purge of the Red Army

In June 1937, Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and seven other senior generals were tried in secret and shot, accused of plotting with Nazi Germany. The purge then ran through the officer corps. Of the Red Army’s eight marshals, five were shot. Of 80 senior army commanders, 75 were executed or imprisoned. Around 35,000 officers in total — perhaps a third of the corps — were removed. The damage was visible four years later: the early disasters of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 partly reflected an army shorn of its experienced leadership.

The NKVD, Yezhov and the Gulag

The institutional driver was the NKVD (the People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs), heir to the Cheka. From September 1936 it was led by Nikolai Yezhov — the ‘Yezhovshchina’ takes its name from him. Yezhov set quotas for arrests by region: each NKVD office had a target number of ‘enemies’ to find. Quotas drove denunciations as ordinary Soviets accused colleagues, neighbours and rivals to deflect attention from themselves.

Most arrested were sent to the gulag: a network of forced-labour camps stretching from Solovki to Kolyma in the Soviet Far East. Conditions were brutal — mining gold or felling timber on starvation rations in Arctic temperatures. Estimates of camp deaths in the late 1930s vary; perhaps a million died of cold, hunger and overwork. By 1939 the gulag held around 1.6 million prisoners and was a significant economic asset, building canals, railways and mines.

Yezhov himself was arrested in November 1938 and shot in 1940. Lavrenti Beria replaced him and wound the Terror down somewhat, though arrests and shootings continued. The pattern — Stalin discarding his own enforcers when they became too associated with the violence — would repeat.

The Terror was not limited to old revolutionaries. Mass operations targeted entire categories: ex-kulaks deported in 1929-30, Polish residents of the USSR (around 110,000 shot in the ‘Polish Operation’ of 1937-38), Germans, Latvians and other minorities, plus engineers, priests and teachers. Roughly 750,000 people were executed in 1936-38, with another million-plus sent to camps. Examiner reports flag students who write ‘only old Bolsheviks were purged’ — this is wrong and loses marks.

Censorship, Socialist Realism and the Cult of Personality

A controlled culture sat alongside the violence. Socialist Realism became the only permitted style in 1934: novels, paintings, films and music had to portray heroic workers, wise leaders and a glorious socialist future. Modernist and experimental art was condemned as ‘formalist’. Photographs were retouched to remove disgraced figures — Trotsky was airbrushed out of pictures of Lenin’s funeral; Yezhov was airbrushed out alongside Stalin once he too was purged. School textbooks rewrote the history of the revolution to put Stalin alongside Lenin.

The cult of personality reached its peak. Stalin’s portraits hung in every classroom, factory and kolkhoz. Streets, cities and a tank model bore his name. The 1936 Constitution proclaimed the most democratic political system in the world — a paper document, since real power lay with Stalin and the Politburo. The cult was not just imposed: ordinary Soviets, including many who lost relatives in the Terror, often genuinely believed Stalin was being deceived by NKVD officials acting on their own authority.

Why? The Historiography

Why did the Terror happen? The two main schools clash sharply.

The totalitarian school, led by Robert Conquest in *The Great Terror* (1968), argues the Purges were driven top-down by Stalin’s personal will to remove rivals and consolidate power. The Terror was deliberate, planned, and centrally directed. Revisionists, led by J. Arch Getty (*Origins of the Great Purges*, 1985) and Sheila Fitzpatrick, argue the Terror grew partly out of bureaucratic chaos, denunciations from below, and conflict between Moscow and the regions. Stalin set the tone, but quotas and local activists shaped the scale. Both schools agree Stalin was responsible — they disagree on whether the violence was a centrally controlled machine or a chain reaction Stalin lost control of and only later contained. Top-band 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation answers can name these schools and use them to test which view a given source is drawing on.

Key Fact

The totalitarian school (Conquest) argues the Terror was driven top-down by Stalin’s personal will. Revisionists (Fitzpatrick, Getty) argue it grew partly from quota culture, denunciations from below and bureaucratic chaos — though Stalin set the political climate that allowed it.

practice_questions.text: How does Interpretation A differ in tone from Interpretation B about Stalin’s role in the Great Terror? Use Interpretations A and B to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A may treat Stalin as the central architect personally directing every stage of the Terror; B may treat the violence as a chain reaction shaped by local quotas and denunciations.
• A may emphasise show trials and the murder of Kirov; B may emphasise NKVD quotas and bureaucratic chaos.
• Specific textual reference required for both.
[4 marks — Mastering: clear comparison of tone with precise textual reference. Secure: comparison with some reference. Developing: paraphrase rather than comparison. Emerging: one interpretation only.]

practice_questions.text: Why might Interpretations A and B give different views about the show trials of the Old Bolsheviks?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Different schools of thought: totalitarian (Conquest) versus revisionist (Fitzpatrick, Getty).
• Different time of writing: pre-1991 (limited archive access) versus post-1991 (NKVD records released).
• Different purposes: a Soviet-era textbook versus a Western academic study.
• Different evidence: trial transcripts versus survivor memoirs and Politburo papers.
[4 marks — Mastering: explains two distinct reasons rooted in purpose, evidence, time of writing or perspective. Secure: one developed reason and one undeveloped. Developing: identifies a reason without explanation. Emerging: describes what the interpretations say rather than why they differ.]

practice_questions.text: How convincing is Interpretation A about the causes of the Great Terror? Use Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Test specific claims of the interpretation against named context: Kirov’s murder December 1934, three Moscow show trials, NKVD quotas under Yezhov, around 750,000 executions in 1936-38.
• Weigh totalitarian readings (Stalin’s personal will) against revisionist accounts (denunciations from below, bureaucratic chaos).
• Cite Conquest or Fitzpatrick and Getty as schools of thought.
• Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. Stalin set the political climate that made the violence possible, but the quota system and local denunciations shaped its scale.
[8 marks — Mastering: precise contextual knowledge tests the interpretation and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: relevant knowledge with clear judgement. Developing: knowledge unevenly linked. Emerging: describes the interpretation without testing it.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the purge of the Red Army officer corps in 1937 on the Soviet Union by 1941.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Loss of experienced leadership: 5 of 8 marshals shot, around 35,000 officers removed.
• Surviving officers afraid to take initiative or report bad news, weakening tactical decision-making.
• Stalin promoted political loyalty over military skill in replacements.
• Contributed to the catastrophic early defeats of Operation Barbarossa in summer 1941.
• Forced rapid emergency promotions during the war (Zhukov, Konev, Rokossovsky) once skilled officers were missing.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the purge.]

practice_questions.text: ‘The Great Terror was driven mainly by Stalin’s personal will to eliminate rivals.’ Evaluate this view. You should consider Stalin’s personal role, the work of the NKVD and other relevant factors, and reach a substantiated judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for Stalin’s personal will (Conquest):
• Personally signed death lists; demanded confessions from Bukharin and others.
• Exploited Kirov’s murder to launch the Terror.
• Used trials to destroy the Old Bolsheviks who had known Lenin.
• Removed and shot Yagoda, then Yezhov, when each had served his purpose.

Arguments for other factors (revisionist):
• Quota culture in the NKVD drove arrests beyond the centre’s explicit list.
• Denunciations from below targeted neighbours, rivals and class enemies.
• Local activists rewarded for finding ‘enemies’; central control was patchy.
• The 1932-33 famine and the strain of collectivisation produced political fear that Stalin could exploit.
• Beria’s appointment in late 1938 wound the worst of the violence down — suggesting it was not pure central control.

Reach a substantiated overall judgement — e.g. Stalin set the political climate and signed the key death lists, but the scale was driven by quotas and local denunciations.
[12 marks — Mastering: developed treatment of two or more factors with substantiated overall judgement. Secure: clear treatment with some judgement. Developing: factors covered without weighing. Emerging: descriptive listing.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the cult of personality on Soviet society in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stalin’s portraits in classrooms, factories and kolkhozes shaped daily public life.
• Socialist Realism in art, novels and film made the cult inescapable culturally.
• Photographs and textbooks rewrote history to remove disgraced figures and place Stalin alongside Lenin.
• Many Soviets genuinely believed Stalin was being deceived by NKVD officials acting alone, sustaining loyalty to him through the Terror.
• Made dissent psychologically as well as politically dangerous — criticism of Stalin felt like criticism of socialism itself.
• Effects should be linked in chains rather than listed.
[8 marks — Mastering: chains of consequence with precise detail. Secure: clear effects with development. Developing: effects identified without development. Emerging: simple description of the cult.]

before.content_html:
For four years from June 1941 the Soviet Union fought the largest land war in history. Roughly 27 million Soviet citizens died — about one in seven. By 1945 Stalin was master of half of Europe and a co-architect of the post-war world. The story of the Great Patriotic War is one of catastrophic early losses, brutal endurance, and a transformation of Stalin’s rule that combined wartime relaxation with renewed terror after victory.

The Nazi-Soviet Pact, 1939

In August 1939, Stalin and Hitler stunned the world by signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact, a non-aggression treaty negotiated by Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov and his German counterpart Joachim von Ribbentrop. Secret protocols divided Eastern Europe into spheres of influence: Stalin took eastern Poland, the Baltic states and parts of Romania; Hitler took western Poland and a free hand against the West. Stalin saw the Pact as buying time and pushing the Soviet border westwards. Hitler always intended to break it.

Operation Barbarossa, June 1941

Stalin received dozens of warnings of an imminent German attack — from British intelligence, his own spies (Richard Sorge in Tokyo, Leopold Trepper’s Red Orchestra), and his front-line generals. He dismissed them as British provocations. On 22 June 1941, three million German and Axis soldiers crossed the Soviet frontier in Operation Barbarossa. The Luftwaffe destroyed most of the Soviet air force on the ground in 24 hours.

Stalin reportedly withdrew to his dacha for several days, possibly expecting to be arrested by his own Politburo. When he eventually addressed the nation by radio on 3 July, he called Soviet citizens ‘brothers and sisters’ — family language not used in Stalin propaganda before. By December 1941 the Germans had reached the suburbs of Moscow. Three million Soviet soldiers had been killed or captured.

Key Fact

Operation Barbarossa launched on 22 June 1941 with three million Axis troops. Stalin had ignored intelligence warnings and the 1937 purges had stripped the army of experienced commanders. By December 1941, three million Soviet soldiers had been killed or captured, and the Germans were at the gates of Moscow.

Mobilising the Home Front

The most dramatic Soviet achievement was industrial. Between July and December 1941, around 1,500 factories were dismantled and shipped east of the Ural Mountains, beyond the reach of German bombers. Workers, mostly women, restarted production on muddy ground in the Urals winter. By 1942, Soviet weapons output exceeded German output. The T-34 tank — faster, better-armoured and easier to produce than its German rivals — became the iconic Soviet weapon of the war.

Female employment surged again. Women drove tractors, ran lathes, served as pilots in the ‘Night Witches’ bomber regiment, and worked as front-line snipers and medics. Around half a million women served in the Red Army. American Lend-Lease — trucks, food, aviation fuel, raw materials — helped: the USSR received over 400,000 trucks and roughly 14,000 aircraft. The relative weight of Lend-Lease versus Soviet production is debated; both mattered.

Leningrad, Stalingrad and Kursk

The siege of Leningrad ran from September 1941 to January 1944 — 872 days. Roughly one million civilians died, mostly of starvation; people ate wallpaper paste, leather and, in extreme cases, the dead. The Battle of Stalingrad, between August 1942 and February 1943, became the war’s turning point. German Sixth Army, encircled by a Soviet pincer movement (Operation Uranus, November 1942), surrendered on 2 February 1943 under Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus — 91,000 prisoners of whom only 5,000 survived to return home in the 1950s.

The Battle of Kursk in July 1943, the largest tank engagement in history, confirmed Soviet superiority. From there, Soviet forces drove west, reaching Berlin in April 1945. Stalin signed the German surrender on 9 May 1945 — Victory Day, still Russia’s most important national holiday.

Stalin’s record as a wartime leader is contested. Early failures — ignoring intelligence, paralysis at Barbarossa, ordering ‘not one step back’ (Order 227 of July 1942) which forbade retreat at Stalingrad on pain of death — cost millions of Soviet lives. Later, he learned to delegate to professionals like Marshal Georgy Zhukov, the most successful Red Army commander, who oversaw victories at Moscow, Stalingrad, Kursk and Berlin. Stalin chaired the State Defence Committee that ran the war effort and made the strategic decisions on factory evacuation. Examiner reports flag the ‘Stalin was always brilliant’ misconception — show you can weigh the early failures against the eventual victory.

Wartime Society

War transformed daily life. Stalin tactically relaxed pressure on the Russian Orthodox Church — reopening churches, releasing imprisoned bishops — to mobilise patriotic feeling. Wartime propaganda emphasised Russian rather than Communist heroes (Alexander Nevsky, Suvorov) and used the term ‘Motherland’ (Rodina) more than ‘socialism’. The Comintern was dissolved in 1943 to reassure the Western Allies. Conditions for ordinary Soviets remained brutal: rationing, conscription, deportation of suspect minorities (Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans) en masse. Famines hit again in 1942-43.

Repression continued alongside this relaxation. Order 270 in 1941 declared every Soviet soldier who surrendered to the enemy a traitor; their families could be punished. SMERSH (counter-intelligence under the NKVD) shot deserters and screened returning prisoners of war. The gulag continued to expand. Wartime relaxation was tactical, not principled — once victory was secured, much of it would be reversed.

From 1941 onwards Stalin deported entire ethnic groups suspected of disloyalty. Volga Germans were uprooted in 1941 within weeks of Barbarossa. Chechens and Ingush were deported from the North Caucasus in February 1944 — around half a million people moved by cattle truck to Kazakhstan and Central Asia in days, with thousands dying of cold and hunger en route. The Crimean Tatars followed in May 1944, accused of collaborating with the German occupiers; nearly a third died in the first year of exile. The deportations show the wartime regime continuing the pre-war logic of collective punishment, even as it relaxed pressure on the Orthodox Church for tactical reasons.

The Cost of Victory

By 1945 the USSR had paid a price beyond comparison. Roughly 27 million Soviet dead, perhaps two-thirds of them civilians. About 1,700 cities and 70,000 villages were destroyed. Industry had to be rebuilt from rubble across European Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. Yet the Soviet Union emerged a superpower — with the Red Army occupying Eastern Europe, atomic-weapon research underway, and a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Stalin was at the height of his international authority. Within a year of victory the wartime alliance with Britain and the United States had collapsed into the Cold War.

Key Fact

The Soviet Union lost roughly 27 million people in the war — about one in seven citizens. The siege of Leningrad lasted 872 days; the German Sixth Army surrendered at Stalingrad on 2 February 1943. The cost was matched by transformation: the USSR emerged a superpower controlling Eastern Europe.
before.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports flag two recurring misconceptions on this period. Don’t write ‘Stalin was always a brilliant wartime leader’ — show you know about Order 227 and the Barbarossa paralysis. Don’t write ‘the USSR won because of Allied aid alone’ — Lend-Lease mattered, but factory evacuation east and Soviet manpower were decisive. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, name historiographical positions: orthodox Soviet readings stress the heroism of the Soviet people; Western readings (some critical, some respectful) weigh Stalin’s role against the Red Army and the home front.
